title: Sumayyah, the first martyr
hookLine: Sumayyah bint Khayyat, killed for her faith, is remembered as the first martyr of Islam
carry: the first to give her life

lines: A FATHER, A MOTHER, A SON.
NO CLAN TO PULL HER AWAY.
cards: A father, a mother, and their son. When Ibn Ishaq comes to the worst of the persecution in Mecca, he names this family together: Yasir, his wife, and their son Ammar.
Men from the clan of Makhzum have taken them out into the heat of the city to make them give up the new faith. The mother has no powerful family to pull her away. Her name is Sumayyah bint Khayyat.
The early biographers give her only a few lines, and tradition has kept those lines and retold them. Today: Sumayyah.

teach.h: A SERVANT, A WIFE, A MOTHER.
teach.b: Start with who she was. The sirah books say she had been a servant in a household of Makhzum. She married Yasir, a man from outside Mecca who lived there under that clan's protection, and they had a son, Ammar.

So when the family became Muslim, nobody stood between them and the clan. Like Bilal yesterday, they had no tribe behind them, and Ibn Ishaq says Quraysh turned hardest on the Muslims who had no clan to protect them.
Ibn Majah reports from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that Sumayyah was among the first to make their Islam public, not just to hold it quietly. Then the end.

teach.h: SHE WOULD ACCEPT NOTHING BUT ISLAM.
teach.b: Ibn Ishaq says the family was tortured in the heat of Mecca, and that Sumayyah was killed because she would accept nothing but Islam.
Ibn Sa'd adds that Abu Jahl, one of the leaders of Quraysh, struck her with a spear, and he calls her the first martyr in Islam.
The Arabic word for martyr is shahid, and the Qur'an uses the same word for a witness. A martyr, in that sense, is someone whose life becomes testimony. Notice how little the sources hand us.
No speech. No last words. Just a choice, held under pressure, by someone the powerful thought did not matter.
Tradition remembers her for it: in Ibn Sa'd's telling, the first life given in Islam was a woman's, and she was not one of the powerful.

how: Muslims remember Sumayyah, the mother of Ammar ibn Yasir, in sirah lessons and sermons on the early persecution in Mecca.

o: a companion who carried the Qur'an to Abyssinia
a wealthy Meccan woman who protected the Prophet
Ammar's mother, remembered as Islam's first martyr

p: mother of Ammar, wife of Yasir
the clan that tortured the family
calls her the first martyr in Islam

s: Sumayyah came from a powerful clan that protected her
the sirah says she had been a servant of Makhzum, with no clan to shield her.
Ibn Ishaq says she was killed because she would accept nothing but Islam
the family was tortured in the heat; she refused to give it up.
the sources record a long last speech from her
they give no speech at all: only her choice, held under pressure.

games.q: you're Sumayyah, out on the hot ground. the men want you to give up your faith. what do you do?
o: say what they want and go home.
refuse, and accept nothing but Islam.
games.why: Ibn Ishaq says she would accept nothing but Islam, and was killed for it. Ibn Sa'd names Abu Jahl as the one who struck her.

practice: Remember someone who suffered for what they believed: someone from history, from any faith or none, or from your own family, like a grandparent who kept their faith quietly in a hard place, or a person who lost a job for refusing to lie.
Hold their face, or just their name, and say it once, softly, keeping them company the way people have kept Sumayyah's name. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Sumayyah. Sumayyah bint Khayyat, mother of Ammar, killed in Mecca for her faith, whom Ibn Sa'd calls the first martyr in Islam. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a martyr; the same word is used in the Qur'an for a witness.

carryVoice: Your line: the first to give her life. A few lines in the old books, and a name still spoken. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (Banu Makhzum torture Ammar, his father and mother; she is killed for refusing anything but Islam)
Ibn Sa'd, Kitab al-Tabaqat al-Kabir (Sumayyah bint Khayyat: struck by Abu Jahl; the first martyr in Islam)
Sunan Ibn Majah 150 (Ibn Mas'ud: those who first made their Islam public, including Sumayyah)
